items: HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; HTTP semantics unchanged
Only the transport is wrapped, not the protocol
TLS sits between TCP (L4) and the application
App writes plaintext; TLS encrypts records under it
Port 443 vs 80 is convention — TLS is not port-bound

blocks.title: The Name 'SSL'
items: SSL is the dead ancestor, disabled everywhere
TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated by RFC 8996 in 2021
'SSL' survives only as slang and in OpenSSL
Confidentiality: eavesdropper cannot read it
Integrity: tampering is detected, not silent
Authentication: server proves its identity
One-way by default — client stays anonymous
Client only proves itself under mTLS

blocks.title: Valid Is Not Honest
blocks.text: A cert on `phishing-site.com` validates perfectly. TLS proves domain control, never trustworthiness.

items: After the handshake, data is chopped into records
Max 16 KB plaintext per record
Each record independently MAC'd or AEAD-sealed
Handshake protocol negotiates the keys
Record protocol carries bulk data with them

blocks.title: Reading The Padlock
blocks.text: `https://` means encrypted and the cert validated. It does not mean the site is safe.

blocks.title: Mixed Content
items: HTTPS page loading an HTTP script = full takeover
Attacker rewrites the DOM from the wire
Browsers block active mixed content outright

blocks.title: Precondition: TCP Done
items: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK already completed
TLS starts on an established byte stream
That TCP RTT is billed before TLS begins
ClientHello: max version, 32-byte client random
Plus session ID and cipher suites, best first
Plus extensions: SNI, ALPN, curves, sig algs
ServerHello: picks exactly ONE suite and version
Plus its own 32-byte server random and session ID

slides.page_title: The TLS 1.2 Handshake, Step by Step

items: Certificate: leaf plus intermediate CAs
Chain order matters; root is normally omitted
ServerKeyExchange: ephemeral ECDHE public key
Signed with the cert's private key — that proves possession
ServerHelloDone: server is finished talking
ClientKeyExchange carries the client ephemeral key
Both sides now compute the same ECDHE secret
Pre-master + both randoms feed the PRF
Out comes the master secret, then session keys
ChangeCipherSpec flips each side to encrypted
Finished carries a hash of the whole transcript
Edit any earlier plaintext message and hashes diverge
Handshake aborts — this is the anti-downgrade check

blocks.title: 3 RTT To First Byte
blocks.text: 1 RTT for TCP plus 2 full RTT of TLS 1.2 handshake before a single byte of application data moves.

items: Static RSA: client encrypts pre-master to server key
No ephemeral key, so no forward secrecy
One stolen key decrypts every past capture
Removed entirely in TLS 1.3

blocks.title: Plaintext Until Done
blocks.text: Everything through ServerHelloDone is in the clear in TLS 1.2 — the certificate and the SNI are both readable on the wire.

items: Client guesses the server's group in ClientHello
`key_share` carries an ephemeral key speculatively
Keys derive one round trip earlier — 1-RTT default
Wrong guess: server sends HelloRetryRequest
That retry costs one extra RTT
Everything after ServerHello is encrypted
That includes the whole certificate chain
Passive observers no longer see your cert
Cipher suites shrank from hundreds to five
They name only the AEAD and the hash
Gone: RSA key transport and static DH
Gone: CBC modes, RC4, 3DES
Gone: MD5 and SHA-1 signatures
Gone: compression and renegotiation
Gone: custom DHE groups — named groups only

blocks.title: Mandatory Now
items: Ephemeral (EC)DHE in every handshake, no exceptions
AEAD-only: AES-GCM, AES-CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305
No encrypt-then-MAC vs MAC-then-encrypt footgun
HKDF replaces the TLS 1.2 PRF
A key schedule derives one secret per stage
Stages: early, handshake, application
A leak at one stage does not unlock the others
0-RTT: app data rides the client's first flight
Zero round trips to the first byte
Price: early data is replayable
Server contributed no freshness to it yet
Send idempotent requests only — GET, never POST
Middlebox mode sends a dummy ChangeCipherSpec
The version field on the wire still says TLS 1.2
Broken middleboxes therefore stop dropping it
1.3 was designed to deploy over today's internet

blocks.title: Downgrade Sentinel
blocks.text: When a server negotiates a lower version it writes a magic value into the last 8 bytes of ServerRandom; the client checks for it.

items: A cert is a signed statement, nothing more
It binds a public key to an identity
The CA signs a hash of the TBSCertificate blob
Change one field and the signature breaks
Subject Alternative Name holds the real hostnames
Browsers ignored Common Name since about 2017
SAN types: dNSName is the common one
Also iPAddress, and rarely email or URI

slides.page_title: Certificate Extensions: KeyUsage, EKU & CA Flags

items: KeyUsage: digitalSignature, keyEncipherment
EKU serverAuth is `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1`
No serverAuth means rejected for HTTPS
BasicConstraints `CA:TRUE` + pathLen marks a CA
A leaf must be `CA:FALSE` or it can mint certs

slides.page_title: Cert Formats, Validation Tiers & Chain Shape

items: DV: proves domain control, minutes, free
OV: the organisation gets vetted
EV: extended vetting, heavy paperwork
Browsers removed the green bar — EV buys no UI

blocks.title: Lifetimes Are Shrinking
items: 825 days, then 398 days in 2020
47 days by industry ballot, phasing to 2029
Manual renewal is dead; automate with ACME
SCTs prove CT logging — Chrome rejects certs without

blocks.title: Self-Signed
blocks.text: Issuer equals subject, signed with its own key. Fine for internal tooling with an explicitly trusted root; never for the public web.

items: Leaf, then intermediates, then a root
Trust flows down, verification walks up
Roots are self-signed and live offline in an HSM
Intermediates do the day-to-day signing
So one compromise does not burn the root

blocks.title: Checked At Each Hop
items: Signature validity against the issuer key
notBefore / notAfter window
basicConstraints `CA:TRUE`, pathLen not exceeded
Revocation status

slides.page_title: Path Building: Walking Up To The Root

items: The root is NOT sent on the wire
It must already be in the client's trust store
Sending it just wastes bytes
Client matches leaf Issuer to an issuer Subject
Verify signature, repeat until a trusted root

slides.page_title: Trust Stores, CT Logs & Broken Chains

items: Per-platform, never universal
Mozilla NSS, Microsoft, Apple, Android
Each has its own policy and update cadence
~150 roots means ~150 orgs can mint for your domain
Any CA in any store can issue for any name
Every public cert must hit append-only CT logs
Mis-issuance becomes detectable after the fact
Monitor your own names on crt.sh or a CT service
That is how you find a cert someone else got
Cross-signing: a new root signed by an old one
One cert, two valid paths, old devices still chain
DST Root X3 expiry (Sept 2021) broke old Android
And OpenSSL 1.0.2 — fine on new clients, dead on old

blocks.title: #1 Production Misconfig
blocks.text: Forgetting to serve the intermediate. Browsers paper over it with AIA fetching and cached intermediates; curl, Java and Go hard-fail.

blocks.title: Revocation Is Broken
items: CRLs are enormous and rarely fresh
OCSP leaks your browsing to the CA
OCSP fails open — the attacker just blocks it
OCSP stapling: server fetches its own response
Then staples it into the handshake
Fixes both the privacy leak and the latency
`Must-Staple` in the cert makes it non-optional

blocks.title: Expiry Is Winning
blocks.text: Short lifetimes beat revocation infrastructure: a 47-day cert is its own expiry mechanism.

blocks.title: Valid Cert, Wrong Site
blocks.text: A perfectly valid cert for `attacker.com` passes chain validation on a connection to `bank.com`. Only the hostname check catches it.

items: One: is the chain cryptographically valid and trusted
Two: does this cert belong to the host I dialed
Clients constantly conflate the two
Skipping step two is the classic silent vuln

caption.text: The padlock does not mean the site is safe — it means the bytes are encrypted to whoever answered the phone. This handbook walks the TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes packet by packet, decodes certificate chains and SAN matching, explains why SNI still leaks every hostname you visit, and ends with the config checklist and error-triage table you actually reach for at 2am. 10 pages, no fluff: internals, trade-offs, and the misconfigurations that bite in production.
